World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Smith given 'every assurance' of LIV survival
World.content:
Former world number two Cameron Smith says he has been given "every assurance" that LIV Golf will continue beyond 2026 as the league works to secure new funding sources.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced last month that it would not continue its financial support of the league beyond this season.

Smith signed with the breakaway league in 2022, receiving a contract reportedly worth $US140 million ($193 million).

He is also the captain of the all-Australian team Ripper GC.

LIV Golf's Adelaide event has been among the league's most popular stops, and he told 10 News that the goal was "definitely" to have the event return in 2027.

Smith, along with fellow LIV Golf stars Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm, turned down an offer to return to the PGA Tour earlier this year, saying in January that "I am here to stay, I'm here to support LIV".

LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil has stated confidence the league would survive in a "multi-partner" format. Whether that comes to fruition and what impact it would have on the league's makeup remains to be seen.

"Since joining LIV, I've learned to live with, you know, speculation," Smith said, while laughing at the notion that he might retire if the league folded.

"I'm 32, so I've got a while yet."

LIV Golf has died on a flawed premise and a broken promise While Adelaide showed just how good LIV Golf could be, the flawed premise of the breakaway tournament always spelled trouble.

Smith has struggled to maintain his form while playing for LIV. His missed cut at the Masters last month was his sixth consecutive at a major.

Despite LIV golfers earning some world rankings points for the first time in 2026, Smith sits at number 235, having posted only two top-10 finishes through the first six events of the season.

However, Smith said his competitive fire remained strong as he prepared for LIV Golf Virginia ahead of next week's PGA Championship.

"I want to win tournaments, I want to win majors," Smith said.

"It's been a while since I've been, you know, truly competitive at the top of the leaderboard. So, the fire is really burning at the moment.

"It feels like I'm getting a lot of confidence back out in the golf once again, which I've struggled with."

Reuters

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: $1b worth of forgotten roads have been 'found' by Queensland councils
World.content:
More than a billion dollars' worth of forgotten roads, footpaths, and drains have been discovered by Queensland councils in the past five years.

A Queensland Audit Office report found that between the 2020 and 2025 financial years, councils reported $1.34 billion in "found assets".

The Local Government 2025/26 report found systemic weaknesses in the way councils kept track of what they owned.

Council documents show that last financial year, the City of Gold Coast found $37.4 million in found assets, and another $41.1 million the year prior.

Their statements also show $27 million worth of assets were "derecognised" because they had accidentally been counted twice, or no longer existed.

A council spokesperson said these were minor errors, considering how many assets they owned.

"The prior period error in 2025 represents approximately 0.17 per cent of [the] council's $22 billion asset base," the spokesperson said.

"While this is small relative to the size of [the] council's overall asset base, it still needed to be corrected as a prior period error."

Forgotten roads

Logan City Council has owned roads in Beaudesert for 18 years without realising it. (Supplied: Philippa Westerman)

Logan City Council discovered $35.8 million in found assets in the 2024 financial year.

A Logan council spokesperson told 612 ABC Brisbane that this included 83 kilometres of unsealed roads and 8.5 kilometres of concrete pavement.

The spokesperson said this was partly related to Logan's amalgamation with parts of the Gold Coast and the former Beaudesert Shire in 2008.

"[The] council continues to strengthen its asset data quality through routine inspection programs, while also progressing a Digital Transformation Program to enhance system integration and support the effective management of the city's assets," the spokesperson said.

Last financial year, Sunshine Coast Regional Council discovered $92 million of assets, including local roads, bridges, stormwater, and parks.

A spokesperson told 612 ABC Brisbane that the council had noticed "differences" between what was on their books and what was on their maps.

The financial year prior, they found another $71 million.

City of Moreton Bay received $56 million in contributed assets last financial year. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

The City of Moreton Bay found $16.5 million in found assets in the 2024 financial year.

A Moreton Bay spokesperson said these were largely "contributed assets", where ownership changed hands between a developer and the council.

Developers can be asked to build public infrastructure in exchange for their buildings being approved.

The spokesperson said there could be some lag time between when these assets were built and when they were inspected and accepted into the council's books.

"City of Moreton Bay is committed to ensuring the timely accounting of all contributed assets, and it must be understood that the completion of construction and assets do not fit a financial year timeframe," the spokesperson said.

World.title: LeBron's new gear at 41 leads lessons from first round of NBA Playoffs
World.content:
After three separate Game 7s to end the first round, the second round of the NBA Playoffs is up and running.

The first round truly had everything you'd want out of the playoffs — just the right amount of spice, a couple of upsets and plenty of contests going down to the wire.

We are down to the final eight teams. Here's what we learnt heading into the conference semifinals.

1. You can never count out LeBron James

LeBron James shows he still has enough juice to carry a team to a playoff series win, even at 41. (Getty Images: Sean M. Haffey)

The Lakers were one of the surprise packets out of the first round, downing the Houston Rockets in a six-gamer.

Coming into the series minus both Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves — the duo widely considered to be the team's best two players this season — the Lakers were rank outsiders against the Rockets.

What betting agencies and experts did not take into account was just how much juice a 41-year-old LeBron James had left in the tank.

James spent the regular season willingly becoming the most over-qualified third banana on the team, even if he wasn't entirely happy with the role. Everyone thought it was because he was no longer capable of being one of the top dogs, but everyone thought wrong.

With both his co-stars out, James seamlessly returned to being the headliner and did what he has done for 23 years: make those around him better.

Luke Kennard turned into a playmaking sniper to start the series, James's son, Bronny, logged key playoff minutes, even outscoring the Rockets bench in a game, while Deandre Ayton showed he wasn't a total lost cause as the Lakers raced out to a 3–0 lead before Reaves's return.

A first-round series win usually isn't consequential when it comes to GOAT debates, but doing what James did against Houston at 41 is another thing Michael Jordan never did. That may or may not be a swing factor, depending on who you talk to.

James is a free agent at the end of the season and there's no telling whether he'll be back on the Lakers, or back in the NBA at all. If he does continue, James could swing the title in the right role on the right team.

2. The Timberwolves might be the NBA's toughest team

Jaden McDaniels (left) and Ayo Dosunmn (right) show there is more to the Timberwolves than their All-NBA guard Anthony Edwards. (Getty Images: David Berding)

The Wolves caused one of the upsets of the first round, ousting the Nuggets despite being obliterated by injuries.

Minnesota lost Donte DiVincenzo to an Achilles injury, Anthony Edwards to a knee and Ayo Dosunmu to a calf injury, yet still managed to close out Nikola Jokic and the Nuggets in six games.

They did so with sheer heart. Jaden McDaniels tempted fate by calling all the Nuggets bad defenders after Game 2 and then walked the walk with a 32-point performance in the close-out game.

Rudy Gobert, he of previous playoff punchlines, reshaped the narrative around his entire career by shackling Jokic in a manner no big man has been able to do in five years.

Minnesota was the living and breathing embodiment of the "next man up" mentality you often hear players talking about.

Terrence Shannon Jr, after averaging just 12.5 minutes a game during the regular season, poured in 24 points to close out the Nuggets and bought himself a regular playoff rotation spot in the process.

Mike Conley, once the best player of the "Grint and Grind" Grizzlies teams from a decade ago, stepped back into the time machine to eat up valuable guard minutes with his star teammates in street clothes.

The Wolves may be undermanned and overmatched, but have proved they'll never be beaten in a series when it comes down to heart and hustle.

3. Joel Embiid still has the top-10 level in him

Joel Embiid (21) showd he still had some MVP-level play left in him as the Sixers oust the Celtics. (Getty Images/The Boston Globe: Danielle Parhizkaran)

Joel Embiid returned from a recent appendectomy to help the 76ers oust the Celtics in a playoff series for the first time since 1982.

Embiid himself had been eliminated by the Celtics on three separate occasions and was desperate to flip the script.

Although his first game back resulted in a heavy loss at home that left the Sixers in a 3–1 hole going into Boston for Game 5, Embiid's final three games of the series were masterful.

Gone were the momentum-killing turnovers when trying to navigate double-teams, or the other turnovers that would come barely from fatigue.

A younger Embiid has also resorted to jacking up untimely threes, a tactic usually born out of fatigue, but played like a proper seven-foot bruiser against the Celtics, and they eventually had no answers.

The 32-year-old was truly the fulcrum of the Sixers offence, not only averaging 28 points but also averaging seven assists per game, and showed enough zip defensively to allow Philadelphia's wing defenders to wreak havoc on the perimeter.

The NBA's great players are defined by their playoff games in close-outs and 34 points, 12 rebounds and six assists to win a road Game 7 as an underdog is just about as legit as it gets. It's a performance that goes down in the Embiid pantheon.

Constant injuries have seen Embiid become an afterthought in top-10 rankings despite winning the MVP three years ago, but this series has been a timely reminder of how special he can be when he is on the court.

4. NBA title windows are fleeting

Jaylen Brown and the Boston Celtics are stunned by the Philadelphia 76ers after going up 3–1. (Getty Images/The Boston Globe: Danielle Parhizkaran)

The NBA is currently searching for its first repeat champion since 2018, when the Golden State Warriors went back to back.

Oklahoma City, last year's champion, is still in the race and is the overwhelming favourite to win the title once again.

However, the demise of the NBA's two previous champs before OKC — Boston and Denver — show that nothing is promised.

The Nuggets looked set to create a new dynasty when they broke through in 2023, but haven't made a conference finals since despite having the player many consider to be the best in the world.

Nikola Jokic (left) and the Denver Nuggets are considering how to best retool after an early playoff exit. (Getty Images: Aaron Ontiveroz)

Denver has lost some of the pieces they surrounded Nikola Jokic with, while the pieces they do have, such as Aaron Gordon, cannot be trusted to stay on the court due to injuries.

The Celtics were forced to blow up their 2024 title-winning core due to salary cap stresses and were sent packing in the first round for the first time since 2021.

Boston still has Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown as its one-two punch, but is trying to figure out who fits best around the All-Star duo, or whether to keep them together at all.

There is more talent than ever and that talent is spread far and wide, making it hard for teams to stack together titles on end like the 90s and 2000s, even if you're a dominant team.

5. The time is now for the Knicks

After knocking on the door for the past few seasons, the Jalen Brunson-era Knicks have their best shot at making the NBA Finals. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

New York found itself in a dogfight against Atlanta in the first round, and three games into the series, things looked downright doomy down 2–1.

To their credit, the Knicks solved the riddle presented by pesky Hawks outfit in Game 4, and it was downhill sledding from thereon.

As the Knicks got on a roll to close the Hawks out on six, their fellow contenders in the Eastern Conference sputtered.

Boston, the favourite to come out of the East, was stunned by a resurgent Philadelphia.

Meanwhile, the other East favourite, Cleveland, eked out an entirely unconvincing win over an undermanned Toronto team, as did the East's top seed, Detroit, which came back from 3–1 down to beat Orlando.

This Knicks core is no stranger to a deep playoff run, having come off a conference finals appearance last year, as well as two semis appearances in the two years prior.

New York has been bounced by Indiana in the last two years, but the Pacers are missing from the playoffs entirely, as is Giannis Antetokounmpo's Milwaukee Bucks.

It is time for the Knicks to reach the finals for the first time since 1999, and it is likely they won't get a better opportunity with this core.

World.title: Call for major banks to invest in First Nations community-led hub
World.content:
A remote Indigenous community in Western Australia's north is calling on the country's biggest banks to put competition aside and collectively invest in a First Nations banking hub.

The proposal, spearheaded by Djarindjin Aboriginal Corporations (DAC) financial counselling service Goolboo Jawal, aims to improve banking accessibility for 2,000 residents who live across the Dampier Peninsula, 2000km north of Perth, regardless of who they bank with.

The banking hub would be based out of Djarindjin and support residents from the four peninsula communities: Djarindjin, Lombadina, Beagle Bay and Ardyaloon (One Arm Point). (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

Goolbool Jawal financial counsellor Veronica Johnson said her pitch to CBA, NAB, Westpac and ANZ would improve culturally appropriate banking services and improve financial literacy at a "grassroots level".

"It is a blueprint for the rest of the First Nation communities," she said.

Ms Johnson said the hub required a "modest" contribution from the banks.

"It's not a lot given the billions of dollars the banks make in profit, to give back to the most vulnerable," she said.

"I think half a million dollars [in total] would get us started and do a pilot."

Veronica Johnson wants ANZ, NAB, Westpac and CBA to invest in a Djarindjin-based culturally appropriate banking hub that would service Dampier Peninsula residents. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

'Changing world of banking'

Ms Johnson said the money would allow DAC to train and employ up to three part-time community members, ultimately reducing residents' need to travel to Broome, amid rising fuel prices.

"It has come to the realisation that we either put food on the table or we travel," she said.

"But one has to work with the other because if you can't access your money, then you can't buy the food."

Dampier Peninsula residents travel hundreds of kilometres to Broome for face-to-face banking support. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

Ms Johnson said while Indigenous banking hotlines and community outreach visits helped, it was not enough in a "changing world of banking".

"Digital [banking] is not exactly appropriate because a lot of the times people may not have the resources," she said.

Residents welcome proposal

Bernadette Angus says travelling to Broome has become a costly experience amid rising fuel prices and cost of living. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

Bardi Jawi elder Bernadette Angus said speaking to someone she knew and trusted in person would be very beneficial.

"If I have problems, they'll know and can see where we're coming from," she said.

"It'd be much easier for us, so we can sit and [they can] talk to us mob and look into things that are difficult for the people here."

Natasha Fejo says she and her colleagues often provide residents with banking support who are unable to wait for telephone support or travel to Broome. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

Aboriginal health worker Natasha Fejo said she often helped residents with online banking.

"That's a big issue … it's hard when you have to go and ask someone to use internet or, the shop has Wi-Fi, but not all people know how to use it," she said.

Residents living at each of the Dampier Peninsula communities, including Beagle Bay, would be able to travel to Djarindjin for banking support. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Beagle Bay community chair Henry Augustine urged the banks to consider the proposal.

"I think it's a great idea," he said.

"We would learn how to use money properly and know what to do with money that may be owing or any money issues."

Watchdog authorisation needed

The hub would work similarly to Bank@Post by Australia Post, which allows customers from 70 financial institutions to withdraw cash or check their account at select regional post offices.

Due to competition laws, the Goolboo Jawal hub and participating banks would need authorisation from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).

An ACCC spokesperson said it "may grant authorisation where proposed conduct is likely to result in a net public benefit".

"Public benefits can include anything of value to the community generally," a ACCC spokesperson said.

ASIC said Goolboo Jawal's banking hub proposal was a creative and interesting idea. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said all banks had an obligation under The Banking Code of Practice to provide inclusive and accessible services to First Nations customers.

ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland said while some "efforts" had been made by a number of banks to improve banking accessibility, remote customers still faced significant barriers.

"Obviously, the advantage of a hub would be to bring together a range of banks in the same place so that regardless of who people bank with, they might be able to access services there," Mr Kirkland said.

" It's ultimately up to the banks whether they think it's appropriate to pursue that idea, but we think it's a really interesting and creative idea. "

The proposal comes almost two years after the financial regulator put Australian banks on notice for causing financial distress, and unfairly charging high fees to low income earners receiving Centrelink payments.

'Don't create dependency'

The ABC contacted ANZ, NAB, Westpac and CBA for comment.

A CBA spokesperson said the bank's focus was on delivering support through "existing services", such as quarterly one to three day visits to Dampier Peninsula communities and the Indigenous Customer Assistance Line.

"We regularly review our visit schedule and where we go with local input as the program expands nationally over the next few years," a CBA spokesperson said.

ANZ, NAB and Westpac did not provide a formal response, but Ms Johnson said one of the banks had shown some support for the proposal.

Ms Johnson said representatives from the four banks visited Djarindjin in April.

"We need to build resilience," she said.

" We need to empower the people so that they're not dependent. Don't create dependency. Empower people to run their own banking hub. "

World.title: Live: US and Iran reportedly exchange fire in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Iranian state media, citing a military official, says Tehran has fired missiles at "enemy units" after a US attack on an Iranian tanker in the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Where have Tasmania's rentals gone? New graph highlights housing problem
World.content:
Tasmania now has less than half the number of vacant rentals than it did a decade ago, according to analysis by Anglicare.

The not-for-profit service provider takes a snapshot of the number of rentals advertised in Tasmania at the end of March each year.

This year, that number was 770.

But 10 years ago there were 1,588 rental properties available.

The month-to-month rental vacancy rate in Tasmania is also dire.

A healthy rental market should have a vacancy rate of about 3 per cent, with anything below that indicating there are generally more people looking for rentals than there are properties available.

Across all regions of Tasmania, the vacancy rate has remained below 1 per cent for more than a year.

So what's causing this? Are there truly fewer homes for rent or is population increase simply outstripping the building of new homes? What about rentals being converted into short-stay accommodation?

Let's take a look.

Experts we spoke to for this story: Peter Phibbs, Emeritus Professor at the University of Sydney

Emeritus Professor at the University of Sydney Ginny Toombs , Anglicare Tasmania's Social Action and Research Centre coordinator

, Anglicare Tasmania's Social Action and Research Centre coordinator Ashleigh Chang , Grattan Institute associate

, Grattan Institute associate Benjamin Price , Housing Institute Australia Tasmania executive director

, Housing Institute Australia Tasmania executive director Michael Kerschbaum, Property Council Tasmania interim executive director

Is population growth to blame?

Peter Phibbs, a Tasmanian-based Emeritus Professor at the University of Sydney who studies housing markets, says Tasmania's rental shortage has three core drivers: population growth, a lack of housing supply, and short-stay accommodation growth.

We'll get to those last two points later.

"We had quite strong population growth in the period from about 2014 until after COVID-19," Professor Phibbs said.

"That placed extra demand pressures on the rental market.

" We really didn't keep up with that increase in population in terms of building new housing supply. "

Tasmania's rental market has continued to tighten while remaining unaffordable for low-income earners. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Taking into account the latest population estimate from the state government, last updated at the end of 2025, Tasmania's population grew from just over 515,000 in 2015, to about 576,000, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics — an increase of almost 12 per cent.

And while Tasmania's population growth outstripped the national average during the COVID years, it has now plunged off a cliff to the worst growth rate in the country, increasing just 0.28 per cent over the past year.

Tasmania's growth rate has significantly lagged behind the rest of the country. (Supplied: Tasmanian Treasury/ABS)

A contributor to this low growth rate is that more people are leaving the state than moving in, while overseas migration remains the lowest in the country.

"While in net terms, Tasmania has lost people to other states, there are other people arriving from other states," Tasmania's executive director of Housing Institute Australia (HIA), Benjamin Price, said.

"When we look at recent years, we haven't done the strategic land use planning on our growing regions across the state to account for that increase in demand."

Benjamin Price, from the Housing Industry Association (HIA), says Tasmania needs more medium-density housing. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Are we not building enough homes?

Each expert the ABC spoke to agreed on one point: at the core of the issue is a mismatch between supply and demand.

"People are using their homes differently, and so we now require more space and more homes than we did in the past," Grattan Institute associate Ashleigh Chang said.

" Despite all this demand, we've simply not built enough homes to keep pace. "

What's missing from the market, Ms Chang said, was medium-density housing — dwelling types between detached dwellings and high-rise apartments.

Tasmania is last in the country for building activity on the HIA's scorecard. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Just last week, the HIA put Tasmania last in the country on its National Housing Scorecard, which measures building activity across each jurisdiction.

It showed "a persistent failure to deliver enough new homes to meet current and future housing demand" in Tasmania.

"You simply cannot address housing affordability or rental shortages without delivering more units and apartments," Mr Price said.

In Tasmania, the problem has been building for several decades, according to Michael Kerschbaum, interim executive director at Property Council Tasmania.

"We almost have to overbuild for a period to deal with that undersupply that's been occurring now for probably a decade or two," Mr Kerschbaum said.

Negative gearing, CGT and trusts explained The government is poised to make changes to negative gearing, the capital gains tax discount and the tax treatment of trusts. So how do they work, and what could changes look like?

Ginny Toombs, Anglicare Tasmania's Social Action and Research Centre coordinator, is frank about the situation in Tasmania.

"What we can say is that Anglicare Tasmania has been doing this for a long time and the situation is getting worse," Ms Toombs said.

"Such a limited supply of properties results in extremely low rental vacancy rates and extreme stress for renters."

How does Hobart compare to other capitals?

The data from other areas across Australia is less clear than Anglicare Tasmania's rental snapshot, though it paints a relatively similar picture on the number of rentals drying up.

In Greater Sydney and the Illawarra, there were about 11,500 listed rentals at the time of the Anglicare Australia Rental Affordability snapshot in 2026, a 9 per cent decrease on the year before and far below pre-pandemic number of 23,000 in 2019.

In Victoria, the figure was sitting at about 15,000 this year, compared to about 19,000 in 2022.

Hobart has fewer rentals available than even a year ago, but so do many other capital cities. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

There were also drops in the number of advertised rentals in Western Australia, the Northern Territory, Brisbane and other regions.

Adelaide was the only major Australian city to record a slight uptick in the number of available rentals, with 8 per cent more listed on the weekend the survey was taken, compared to the same time last year.

"Alot of the other capital cities got past the rental supply problem by building alot of apartment buildings," Professor Phibbs said.

"Apartment buildings are sometimes very good generators of rental properties, but in a place like Hobart, we've really only got a trickle of apartments in the last few years."

Greater Sydney now has half the number of rentals advertised as available compared to 2019. (ABC News: Jack Ailwood)

Are too many rentals becoming short-stay houses?

The amount of short-stay accommodation in Tasmania, like those listed on Airbnb and Stayz, has continued to increase in recent years.

According to the Tasmanian Council of Social Service, there were 3,112 short-stay homes listed (where the entire dwelling is rented out, not just a bedroom in someone's house) in the state in 2019.

In 2024 — which is when the Tasmanian government last released short-stay accommodation data — there were 3,918.

The government has yet to release any more recent data, something independent MP Helen Burnett has pushed the government to do.

Council locks in 1,050 per cent short-stay conversion fee hike A Tasmanian council has pushed through a 1,050 per cent increase in fees for applications to turn a property into short-stay accommodation.

"Every home turned into a short-term accommodation is no longer available in the longer term rental market," Grattan Institute's Ms Chang said.

"But I wouldn't treat short-term stays as a main lever, when the main lever is building more housing, and I wouldn't treat it as a substitute for broader supply reform."

Where short-stay reform matters most is in the areas already struggling with housing supply.

"In those areas we'd say it's worth having reform that disincentivises the use of homes for short-term rental if that area is supply scarce," Ms Chang said.

Hobart City Council has long opposed the increase in short-stay accommodation across the city, arguing it has contributed to a shortage of available and affordable housing.

It receives about 85 applications a year to change a property into short-stay accommodation.

Short-stay levy passes Tasmania's lower house Tasmania is one step closer to introducing a levy on short-stay accommodation, after legislation passed the lower house.

This month, it bumped up the fee to change a property to short-stay accommodationfrom $435 to $5,000, and in 2023 doubled council rates for short-stay properties.

The Tasmanian government is also looking at curtailing the short-stay sector to support housing supply.

On Thursday, legislation passed the lower house to impose a 5 per cent levy to be paid by those renting outshort-stay properties. But the measure, if it passes the upper house, isn't aimed specifically at renters.

All of the revenue, an estimated $8-10 million per year, would go towards covering the cost of exempting first-home buyers from paying stamp duty on existing homes.

Anglicare Tasmania wants the Tasmanian government to directly target that revenue towards social housing instead.

Might the upcoming federal budget make things worse?

The Albanese government is expected to introduce changes to wind back negative gearing and capital gains tax in its upcoming federal budget.

Both tax measures currently make rental properties an attractive vehicle to invest in, giving tax advantages for holding onto a loss-making investment home.

CGT, negative gearing and trust taxes to change The government is still finalising the details of its budget, but several sources say three tax policies that featured in Labor's 2019 election campaign will be revived and rethought.

While the exact details of any wind back have yet to be announced, Mr Kerschbaum says he believes changes will make it less attractive for investors to purchase an investment property, in turn reducing the amount of rentals on the market.

"That will make that asset class less attractive and it'll turn investors away from the property market and potentially into other asset classes," he said.

However, the Grattan Institute's Ms Chang said if capital gains tax was halved and negative gearing curbed, the impact on rents would most likely be small.

"The gain you can get can be redirected to other reform, like rent assistance, which we see as the number one priority to help low income renters," she said.

Ms Toombs said the government had an opportunity in the federal budget to reform the system by winding back tax concessions for investors and instead investing in building more homes.

What can be done to fix this?

Ultimately, it's an issue of supply and incentive.

"Creating more housing is certainly the solution to the problem," Mr Kerschbaum said.

"Whatever we can do to deliver that will help, ultimately, with things like rental affordability and housing affordability."

The lack of available rentals is causing "extreme stress" for Tasmanian renters, Anglicare Tasmania says. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Infill accommodation — housing built on redeveloped or existing land with existing urban areas — needed to be part of the solution, he said.

That includes building more apartments, and medium-density developments.

"We think there's probably just not enough incentive there to do that form of building," Mr Kerschbaum said.

Commissioner issues housing affordability warning Productivity Commissioner Danielle Wood says Australia will not meet the federal government's 1.2 million new home target.

HIA Tasmania has issued its own wishlist of changes to meet demand: faster and more predictable planning approvals; a stronger pipeline of build-ready land; reforms to enable multi-unit and medium-density housing; lower regulatory and compliance costs; and better coordination between housing, infrastructure and population planning.

It's an issue Tasmanian Housing Minister Kerry Vincent is acutely aware of when asked about rental availability and short-stay accommodation in parliament this week.

"I'm laying awake for many hours of the night reading and understanding and listening to everything I possibly can to fine-tune everything that's in my ministry to deliver more homes," he said.

World.title: Dressing room fight leaves Real Madrid captain in hospital
World.content:
Real Madrid's simmering tensions have spilled over, with Federico Valverde and Frenchman Aurélien Tchouaméni involved in a dressing-room fight.

Uruguayan Valverde was taken to hospital with a cut head, several club sources said.

Real later confirmed that team captain Valverde, who was subsequently discharged, suffered a head injury and will be sidelined for up to two weeks.

"Following tests carried out today on our player Fede Valverde by Real Madrid's medical team, he has been diagnosed with a head trauma," the club said in a statement.

"Valverde is at home and in good condition; he will need to rest for between 10 and 14 days, in line with medical protocols for this diagnosis."

The incident unfolded at the club's Valdebebas training ground on Thursday, local time, the day after an earlier altercation between the pair.

The pair more often tackle other players, not each other… (Getty Images: Xinhua/Cheng Min)

A Real Madrid spokesperson told Reuters he would not comment on what happens inside the changing room, but the club later said disciplinary proceedings have been opened against both players.

"Real Madrid announces that, following the incidents that took place this morning during the first-team training session, it has decided to open disciplinary proceedings against our players Federico Valverde and Aurélien Tchouaméni," a statement said.

"The club will announce the outcomes of both cases in due course, once the relevant internal procedures have been completed."

Valverde later posted a statement on social media apologising to the club and its supporters but denied that things got out of hand with a teammate and said that during "an argument" he had "accidentally knocked over a table".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The gravity of the episode prompted an emergency meeting attended by senior club officials, with no players leaving the training ground for over an hour.

The aim was to try to halt an escalation of tensions that has left nerves frayed and the squad divided at a sensitive moment for the team.

The unrest follows another flashpoint earlier this week, when defender Álvaro Carreras acknowledged he had been involved in a heated argument with a teammate but insisted it was "a one-off incident of no significance that has been resolved," after Spanish media reported an alleged incident between him and the club's German defender, Antonio Rüdiger.

Madrid's season has unravelled on multiple fronts. Manager Xabi Alonso was sacked midway through the campaign, and his successor Álvaro Arbeloa has been unable to prevent the team sliding towards a second successive year without a trophy.

Following a Champions League quarter-final exit to Bayern Munich, Real trail LaLiga leaders Barcelona by 11 points with four matches remaining. The sides meet at the Camp Nou on Sunday in a Clasico that could seal the title for the Catalans.

Reuters

World.title: Bin night across Australia is changing as councils, households fight waste
World.content:
A waste expert says Australian households are the "piggy in the middle" of a global "cheap" plastics industry and a local push to reduce the country's waste.

Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed Australia produced about 13 million tonnes of household waste in the 2022-23 financial year.

Much of that household waste is collected by local councils, which pay contractors to collect bins and pay to establish, fill and cap landfill.

Adelaide University's Robert Crocker says people are taking on more responsibility with waste. (Supplied: Adelaide University)

Adelaide University waste expert Robert Crocker said as costs rose for councils, diverting waste away from landfill was one way to manage budgets and meet environmental targets.

But Dr Crocker said it meant more responsibility was being placed on households.

"What people are beginning to find is that the waste problem is so great that there's a pushback from the waste managers saying, 'We can't deal with this anymore, you've got to make a few changes,'" Dr Crocker said.

"Unfortunately the household is in the middle.

" They're like the piggy in the middle between the producers who often just don't care, they just want to sell stuff, and the waste manager that has to actually deal with the outcome. "

Councils watching costs

While waste collection programs differ by state and council, many run a system where a general waste bin is collected weekly, while a recycling bin and green organic waste bin alternate each week.

But as local governments look to divert waste from landfill, some are making changes to encourage more recycling and composting.

Organic bins, known as green or FOGO (food organics and garden organics) bins, have become the focus of new waste management services in South Australia. (ABC South West WA: Jacqueline Lynch)

In South Australia, some councils are running trials of organic bins being collected weekly, with general waste bins moving to fortnightly pick-ups.

Local Government Association of South Australia president Heather Holmes-Ross said it costs council's far more to dump waste in landfill.

"Councils want to get as much kitchen waste out of the landfill bins and into the green bin," she said.

"The issue is then if your green bin is being emptied fortnightly and your landfill bin weekly, you've got this green organic waste building up for two weeks.

Heather Holmes-Ross says trials of alternative waste collection in the state have been positive so far. (Supplied: Local Government Association of South Australia)

"That's when things becoming problematic."

Currently, SA legislation mandates councils offer weekly general waste pick-up, but Dr Holmes-Ross said the sector wanted it to be amended to allow weekly organics bin pick-up.

"Once people are educated about it, they like the idea of helping and being environmentally friendly," she said.

" They also like that it will cost their council less and that should be reflected in their rates notices. "

Smelly bin concerns

The City of Mount Gambier, in South Australia's South East, has voted to commence weekly organic bin pick-ups from mid-2028.

An internal report showed it cost the council about $3.6 million to establish a landfill cell and about $1.2 million to cap it once full.

It also cited an internal audit that found more than 60 per cent of the contents of general waste bins could either be recycled or placed in organic bins.

Most SA councils offer three bins: general waste, green organics and recycling. (Supplied)

The move caused a stir in the local community though, with residents worried it will lead to smelly waste piling up across a fortnight, as well as representing a reduction in council services.

Mount Gambier and District Ratepayers Association president Frank Wilcox said the decision failed to consider large families.

"There's a lot of people in this city, not only businesses, but also people with flats and that sort of thing, who don't have any green areas, that really don't have any green waste," he said.

Mount Gambier is South Australia's largest regional city. (ABC South East SA: Bec Whetham)

"So they would need regular pick-ups on a weekly basis, you would think, plus also young families with children with things like dirty nappies and that sort of thing,

"All the extra waste you get from having children, they need a general pick-up every week."

A 'wasteful' system

Professor Crocker said local governments looking at alternative ways to deal with household waste was a positive.

But he said all stakeholders needed to be more aware of how we generate, separate and dispose of waste to create lasting change.

"From a household point of view, there's almost nothing the individual can do except try to do the best they can," he said.

"And that means being aware that the larger system is ridiculously wasteful.

"You can't blame individuals, you can't blame the government, you have to actually see it as a by-product of our economic system."

Two Islamic State-linked women have been charged with slavery-related offences after landing in Melbourne on Thursday night. Grandmother Kawsar Abbas, 54, and 31-year-old daughter Zeinab were among four women and nine children who arrived in Sydney and Melbourne amid a political debate over whether they should have been permitted to return home to Australia. Chaotic scenes at Melbourne Airport as IS-linked women and children arrive from Syria. Getty Images On Friday morning the pair were charged with enslavement, and using a slave. Kawsar was also charged with possessing a slave and engaging in slave trading. The offences each carry a maximum penalty of 25 years imprisonment. “It will be alleged the woman travelled to Syria in 2014 with her family and knowingly kept a female slave in the home,” the Australian Federal Police said in a statement.



The mother and daughter were taken into police custody after arriving at Melbourne Airport. They are expected to face Melbourne Magistrates Court on Friday. The women arrived from Syria, where they had been living in the al-Roj refugee camp for seven years after leaving Australia to join their partners, who were involved with Islamic State. They were detained in the camp by Kurdish forces in March 2019, the AFP said. Kawsar travelled to Syria with Zeinab and her other daughter Zahra to join her husband, their father, Muhammad Ahmed. The fourth woman who returned to Australia was not arrested. The children will be placed into anti-radicalisation programs and given psychological support as they begin a new life in Australia after spending most of their lives in war zones and decrepit camps.



AFP Assistant Commissioner Counter Terrorism, Stephen Nutt, said investigation was active and involved “very serious allegations”. Victoria Police Assistant Commissioner Martin O’Brien said the safety of all Victorians remains paramount. “Victoria Police will continue to work closely with our law enforcement partners and other agencies to ensure there is no risk to our local community,” he said. “We want to reassure all Victorians that anyone residing in our state who has committed serious criminal offences, including those returning from conflict areas, will be held to account.” The women’s return has been subject of a heated political debate, with the government insisting it had no role in their repatriation and that it could do little to intervene as the women were Australian citizens.



Nationals Leader Matt Canavan said on Friday morning that the government should have accessed special powers to deny the women entry. “We offered to give the government more powers that were rejected,” he told ABC Radio National. “I think what’s really important now is that the prime minister come out today and explain how this has helped … and he should explain to Australian people how he’s keeping them safe.”

World.title: The moment that showed why this player is the ‘Unicorn’
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 The moment that showed why this player is the ‘Unicorn’ Marc McGowan Updated May 8, 2026 — 8:08am ,first published 12:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

This was supposed to be remembered as Jack Gunston’s night. Hawthorn’s seemingly ageless spearhead – an All-Australian with 73 goals at age 33 last year – took eight marks and kicked five of his six majors in the first half on Thursday night to propel his side to a 15-point lead over Fremantle that grew to 22 midway through the third term. Jack Gunston’s six goals could not deny Fremantle from an eighth consecutive win. AFL Photos The only player who seemed capable of stealing the limelight from Gunston was his little mate, Nick Watson, whose wizardry was again on display with some brilliant moments and three goals of his own to half-time. But an opponent nicknamed “the Unicorn”, ruckman Luke Jackson, had other ideas – inspiring the Dockers to a 15-point triumph in Perth that extended their winning streak to eight games and sees them provisionally replace Sydney on top of the AFL ladder.



Related Article Money Talks

AFL 2026 These top picks were supposed to be Essendon’s future. They could be out the door Hawthorn lost defender Tom Barrass (hamstring) in the second quarter, and hung on for dear life as the momentum swung wildly until the dam wall finally burst. Fremantle’s avalanche included 22 inside 50s to the Hawks’ four in the last term, but it took until the final four minutes for them to hit the front. With time running out, Jackson – who played a critical role in Melbourne’s drought-ending 2021 premiership victory – twice intervened in critical contests to help set up Michael Frederick’s game-turning goals. In between, the athletic Jackson, the perfect prototype for the league’s new ruck rules, also won a crucial centre clearance that led to another goal to Hayden Young.



Jackson held off Josh Weddle with his right hand, and gathered the Sherrin with his left, at the top of the 50-metre arc to set up the first of Frederick’s finishes, before his diving smother on Jai Newcombe’s attempted kick on the wing minutes later proved the key moment. View post on X Ruckmen are not supposed to be able to do things like that. Fremantle ruckman Luke Jackson was the match-winner. AFL Photos Instead of Hawthorn going into attack, the Dockers rushed forward through Murphy Reid, and a clever tap from Jye Amiss found Frederick, who slotted what was effectively the sealing goal.



It was an extended run of “Wharfie time”, as the locals call it, that left Hawks coach Sam Mitchell glum-faced, whereas Jackson was joking with his teammates that he was “built different”. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Lion hit with four-match ban for homophobic slur; Bombers dump out-of-form McKay The numbers are Jackson’s evidence: 22 disposals, 18 contested possessions, 10 tackles, seven clearances, 22 hitouts and nine score involvements. He had nine touches, three clearances and five score involvements in the last quarter alone, and might be the man to end his old teammate Max Gawn’s All-Australian ruck monopoly. “We got what we wanted for the majority of the game, and then late, we played into their hands with a bit of the way we played, and some of their good players stood up,” Mitchell said.



“I think it was 0-6 [from] centre bounce, so we couldn’t get any field position, or any composure on the ball. They played well, and deserved to win. “We got taught a bit of a lesson late. We’ve talked a lot this year about being ready to play and win against the best sides, and we proved tonight that we’re not quite there.” It was a third thriller in a month for Hawthorn, who will finish round nine in third spot after a draw and defeat in the past fortnight. Nick Watson might already be the best small forward in the AFL. AFL Photos Mitchell forecast a stint on the sidelines for Barrass, joining fellow injured first-choice Hawks Will Day, Mabior Chol and Calsher Dear, but there are positives to make the flight home easier. They still look the best of the Victorian premiership contenders.



After a quiet night against Collingwood, the now 34-year-old Gunston blitzed Fremantle out of the goal square and forced Justin Longmuir to shift Brennan Cox onto him before quarter-time after Luke Ryan struggled to contain him. Related Article AFL 2026 Ross Lyon saw this trend before it happened. Now his Saints have the weapons to fire His leading patterns remain elite, and he has always been a sharpshooter, although he ended the night with a sore right foot. Gunston’s sixth goal gave Hawthorn a 19-point buffer almost 12 minutes into the fourth quarter, continuing a remarkable resurgence since he returned from an injury-marred gap year at Brisbane in a 2023 trade. Mitchell had warned he might have to play some VFL footy in his second stint in brown and gold, and that eventuated in the early rounds of 2024 – but it soon became obvious that he still had plenty to give.



Gunston’s night out means he at least temporarily leapfrogs Gold Coast’s Ben King to lead the Coleman Medal with 30 goals, plus 19 behinds, from eight matches. View post on X As for Watson, he is in pole position for a maiden All-Australian berth. His dancing feet, unerring defensive effort, sublime skills and general brilliance make for captivating viewing. He might already be the league’s best small forward and most exciting player. Co-captain Jai Newcombe should be in Brownlow Medal contention this season, but equally important is fellow midfielder Cam Mackenzie’s significant development. Jai Newcombe is putting together another strong season. AFL Photos



The Hawks’ other captain, star defender James Sicily, is still the first player opposition coaches devise plans for. Magpie Steele Sidebottom went to him last week, and this time it was Patrick Voss, before Sicily manned Josh Treacy after Barrass’ injury. But Mitchell won’t be too glowing of his on-ball brigade as a unit, given their Dockers counterparts – led by Caleb Serong and Andrew Brayshaw – won the clearances 41-29, including 13-9 out of the centre. Hawthorn looked scintillating with their ball movement in the first half-and-a-bit, but it was always going to be difficult to rely on transitioning from defence all night. Fremantle did a much better job after that of clamping down and forcing the Hawks into long kicks down the line. Mitchell would also love to be getting more out of swingman Josh Weddle, who scored a fat four-year contract for himself in February after Essendon tried to prise him out of the club.



Mitchell said it himself: Hawthorn are good, but not quite good enough yet. The winter months will be vital to whether they can change that in time to win more silverware. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: A new North star? England cricket turn to Australian as new selector
World.content:
SportCricketEngland A new North star? England cricket turn to Australian as new selector Will Macpherson and Nick Hoult May 8, 2026 — 7:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

England are poised to turn to an Australian as their new national selector, with Durham director of cricket Marcus North in line to land the job this week. North, who played 21 Tests for Australia, including two Ashes series, between February 2009 and December 2010, appears to have beaten off competition from former England fast bowlers Steven Finn and Darren Gough to land the job after final interviews. He is expected to accept and his appointment is likely to be confirmed in the coming days. Marcus North playing a shot against England in the 2009 Ashes series. Getty Images North would effectively replace Luke Wright, who stepped down in the wake of last winter’s Ashes for family reasons, citing the strain of so much travel. Wright’s job title was England selector, while North would fill the apparently more senior position of national selector, which has not existed for five years since Ed Smith was made redundant. Smith has gone full circle and will join the ECB board later this year. While England have had plenty of foreign coaches, including incumbent Brendon McCullum, West Australian North would be the first man not from these shores to be charged with selecting the national team.



North’s appointment is a nod to the county game. He played for five counties and has been in charge of cricket at Durham for the past eight years. Since the start of 2025, he has been in charge of the men’s and women’s programmes at the county and he is well regarded in the game. Marcus North (right) with Durham coach Ryan Campbell. North has running the English county for eight years. Getty Images Under his watch, Durham have recovered from the devastation of their enforced relegation for financial reasons in 2016 and looked to be re-establishing themselves in the top flight until a surprise relegation last September. They have started the new Division Two season well and have steadily supplied England with players in recent years, including four members of last winter’s Ashes party. Top-order batsmen Emilio Gay and Ben McKinney are among those vying for a Test cap this summer. Finn, a former team-mate of McCullum at Middlesex, was a prime candidate, but North’s background in administration and work in the county game appear to have secured him the role. Finn, like director of cricket Rob Key, would have been coming into the job from a career in broadcasting. North has lived in the North East for years, having met his wife while playing for Gateshead Fell Cricket Club in 2000. After retiring, he was director of cricket at South Northumberland before getting the job at Durham, where he succeeded Geoff Cook in late 2018. Alongside his role with Durham, he worked as Northern Superchargers’ – now called Sunrisers Leeds – director of cricket in the early years of the Hundred.



Marcus North celebrates scoring a century in the fourth Ashes Test in 2009 in Leeds. Getty Images North has worked with Test captain Ben Stokes at Durham and white-ball captain Harry Brook at the Superchargers, where he also appointed Andrew Flintoff as head coach. Flintoff is now in charge of England Lions, the second-string team, and will be working closely with North. North is expected to be in position in time to help select England’s first squads of the summer next week. These include the Test squad to face New Zealand from June 4, and a Lions group to take on South Africa A from May 22. North is close to Ben Stokes. But the selector’s job is a wider brief than the Test team. It covers white-ball cricket, which is outside of Stokes’s remit and all levels below. North will share similar opinions to Stokes about the direction of the Test team and gives the captain a powerful ally as he looks to stamp his authority on the team and drive them forward in a different style. Stokes may have healed the rift with McCullum – we shall see on that one – but they shared different views on the team’s future not that long ago and how they should play. North will share much of Stokes’s vision.



North knows the county game inside out, not only players but also his fellow directors of cricket and head coaches, which will improve communication. He can heal the rifts that have developed over the last three years and bring an outsider’s perspective to the England environment that from the outside has looked like an echo chamber. Ben Stokes looks on as Australia celebrates Ashes success in Sydney. Getty Images He is the most English of Australians after spending a decent chunk of the past 20 years in county and club cricket as a player, coach and director of cricket. He was also second to Rob Key for the job of England director of cricket four years ago. His appointment to this role puts him in an ideal position to take over when Key steps down. One of the failings of the Ashes series acknowledged by the England and Wales Cricket Board was the lack of planning for the Australia tour, which they blame on several factors. Most important in their eyes was the lack of experience within the governing body of organising Ashes tours. Almost all had left after the 2021-22 trip and the subsequent change in leadership at the top of the ECB.



North played 21 Tests for Australia and will be in position to ensure proper planning for the next Ashes tour in 2029-30, which may well have helped win him the job ahead of the other candidates. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket The $4 million man: Cummins offered monster deal as rivals come after cricket stars Durham’s relegation last year took a little shine off the good work, but it has to be remembered North and chief executive Tim Bostock picked the club up at a very difficult time, with the county broke and relegated as punishment for financial difficulties. It was a major achievement to get them back up into Division one at all. North has experience of rebuilding work. That will be handy. The Telegraph

AFL Photos Instead of Hawthorn going into attack, the Dockers rushed forward through Murphy Reid, and a clever tap from Jye Amiss found Frederick, who slotted what was effectively the sealing goal.



It was an extended run of “Wharfie time”, as the locals call it, that left Hawks coach Sam Mitchell glum-faced, whereas Jackson was joking with his teammates that he was “built different”. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Lion hit with four-match ban for homophobic slur; Bombers dump out-of-form McKay The numbers are Jackson’s evidence: 22 disposals, 18 contested possessions, 10 tackles, seven clearances, 22 hitouts and nine score involvements. He had nine touches, three clearances and five score involvements in the last quarter alone, and might be the man to end his old teammate Max Gawn’s All-Australian ruck monopoly. “We got what we wanted for the majority of the game, and then late, we played into their hands with a bit of the way we played, and some of their good players stood up,” Mitchell said.



“I think it was 0-6 [from] centre bounce, so we couldn’t get any field position, or any composure on the ball. They played well, and deserved to win. “We got taught a bit of a lesson late. We’ve talked a lot this year about being ready to play and win against the best sides, and we proved tonight that we’re not quite there.” It was a third thriller in a month for Hawthorn, who will finish round nine in third spot after a draw and defeat in the past fortnight. Nick Watson might already be the best small forward in the AFL. AFL Photos Mitchell forecast a stint on the sidelines for Barrass, joining fellow injured first-choice Hawks Will Day, Mabior Chol and Calsher Dear, but there are positives to make the flight home easier. They still look the best of the Victorian premiership contenders.



After a quiet night against Collingwood, the now 34-year-old Gunston blitzed Fremantle out of the goal square and forced Justin Longmuir to shift Brennan Cox onto him before quarter-time after Luke Ryan struggled to contain him. Related Article AFL 2026 Ross Lyon saw this trend before it happened. Now his Saints have the weapons to fire His leading patterns remain elite, and he has always been a sharpshooter, although he ended the night with a sore right foot. Gunston’s sixth goal gave Hawthorn a 19-point buffer almost 12 minutes into the fourth quarter, continuing a remarkable resurgence since he returned from an injury-marred gap year at Brisbane in a 2023 trade. Mitchell had warned he might have to play some VFL footy in his second stint in brown and gold, and that eventuated in the early rounds of 2024 – but it soon became obvious that he still had plenty to give.



Gunston’s night out means he at least temporarily leapfrogs Gold Coast’s Ben King to lead the Coleman Medal with 30 goals, plus 19 behinds, from eight matches. View post on X As for Watson, he is in pole position for a maiden All-Australian berth. His dancing feet, unerring defensive effort, sublime skills and general brilliance make for captivating viewing. He might already be the league’s best small forward and most exciting player. Co-captain Jai Newcombe should be in Brownlow Medal contention this season, but equally important is fellow midfielder Cam Mackenzie’s significant development. Jai Newcombe is putting together another strong season. AFL Photos



The Hawks’ other captain, star defender James Sicily, is still the first player opposition coaches devise plans for. Magpie Steele Sidebottom went to him last week, and this time it was Patrick Voss, before Sicily manned Josh Treacy after Barrass’ injury. But Mitchell won’t be too glowing of his on-ball brigade as a unit, given their Dockers counterparts – led by Caleb Serong and Andrew Brayshaw – won the clearances 41-29, including 13-9 out of the centre. Hawthorn looked scintillating with their ball movement in the first half-and-a-bit, but it was always going to be difficult to rely on transitioning from defence all night. Fremantle did a much better job after that of clamping down and forcing the Hawks into long kicks down the line. Mitchell would also love to be getting more out of swingman Josh Weddle, who scored a fat four-year contract for himself in February after Essendon tried to prise him out of the club.



Mitchell said it himself: Hawthorn are good, but not quite good enough yet. The winter months will be vital to whether they can change that in time to win more silverware. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: A new North star? England cricket turn to Australian as new selector
World.content:
SportCricketEngland A new North star? England cricket turn to Australian as new selector Will Macpherson and Nick Hoult May 8, 2026 — 7:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

England are poised to turn to an Australian as their new national selector, with Durham director of cricket Marcus North in line to land the job this week. North, who played 21 Tests for Australia, including two Ashes series, between February 2009 and December 2010, appears to have beaten off competition from former England fast bowlers Steven Finn and Darren Gough to land the job after final interviews. He is expected to accept and his appointment is likely to be confirmed in the coming days. Marcus North playing a shot against England in the 2009 Ashes series. Getty Images North would effectively replace Luke Wright, who stepped down in the wake of last winter’s Ashes for family reasons, citing the strain of so much travel. Wright’s job title was England selector, while North would fill the apparently more senior position of national selector, which has not existed for five years since Ed Smith was made redundant. Smith has gone full circle and will join the ECB board later this year. While England have had plenty of foreign coaches, including incumbent Brendon McCullum, West Australian North would be the first man not from these shores to be charged with selecting the national team.



North’s appointment is a nod to the county game. He played for five counties and has been in charge of cricket at Durham for the past eight years. Since the start of 2025, he has been in charge of the men’s and women’s programmes at the county and he is well regarded in the game. Marcus North (right) with Durham coach Ryan Campbell. North has running the English county for eight years. Getty Images Under his watch, Durham have recovered from the devastation of their enforced relegation for financial reasons in 2016 and looked to be re-establishing themselves in the top flight until a surprise relegation last September. They have started the new Division Two season well and have steadily supplied England with players in recent years, including four members of last winter’s Ashes party. Top-order batsmen Emilio Gay and Ben McKinney are among those vying for a Test cap this summer. Finn, a former team-mate of McCullum at Middlesex, was a prime candidate, but North’s background in administration and work in the county game appear to have secured him the role. Finn, like director of cricket Rob Key, would have been coming into the job from a career in broadcasting. North has lived in the North East for years, having met his wife while playing for Gateshead Fell Cricket Club in 2000. After retiring, he was director of cricket at South Northumberland before getting the job at Durham, where he succeeded Geoff Cook in late 2018. Alongside his role with Durham, he worked as Northern Superchargers’ – now called Sunrisers Leeds – director of cricket in the early years of the Hundred.



Marcus North celebrates scoring a century in the fourth Ashes Test in 2009 in Leeds. Getty Images North has worked with Test captain Ben Stokes at Durham and white-ball captain Harry Brook at the Superchargers, where he also appointed Andrew Flintoff as head coach. Flintoff is now in charge of England Lions, the second-string team, and will be working closely with North. North is expected to be in position in time to help select England’s first squads of the summer next week. These include the Test squad to face New Zealand from June 4, and a Lions group to take on South Africa A from May 22. North is close to Ben Stokes. But the selector’s job is a wider brief than the Test team. It covers white-ball cricket, which is outside of Stokes’s remit and all levels below. North will share similar opinions to Stokes about the direction of the Test team and gives the captain a powerful ally as he looks to stamp his authority on the team and drive them forward in a different style. Stokes may have healed the rift with McCullum – we shall see on that one – but they shared different views on the team’s future not that long ago and how they should play. North will share much of Stokes’s vision.



North knows the county game inside out, not only players but also his fellow directors of cricket and head coaches, which will improve communication. He can heal the rifts that have developed over the last three years and bring an outsider’s perspective to the England environment that from the outside has looked like an echo chamber. Ben Stokes looks on as Australia celebrates Ashes success in Sydney. Getty Images He is the most English of Australians after spending a decent chunk of the past 20 years in county and club cricket as a player, coach and director of cricket. He was also second to Rob Key for the job of England director of cricket four years ago. His appointment to this role puts him in an ideal position to take over when Key steps down. One of the failings of the Ashes series acknowledged by the England and Wales Cricket Board was the lack of planning for the Australia tour, which they blame on several factors. Most important in their eyes was the lack of experience within the governing body of organising Ashes tours. Almost all had left after the 2021-22 trip and the subsequent change in leadership at the top of the ECB.



North played 21 Tests for Australia and will be in position to ensure proper planning for the next Ashes tour in 2029-30, which may well have helped win him the job ahead of the other candidates. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket The $4 million man: Cummins offered monster deal as rivals come after cricket stars Durham’s relegation last year took a little shine off the good work, but it has to be remembered North and chief executive Tim Bostock picked the club up at a very difficult time, with the county broke and relegated as punishment for financial difficulties. It was a major achievement to get them back up into Division one at all. North has experience of rebuilding work. That will be handy. The Telegraph
